newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF AGREES $657 MILLION LOAN TO BAIL OUT BULGARIA.
newsitem.headline: IMF AGREES $657 MILLION LOAN TO BAIL OUT BULGARIA.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund has agreed a $657 million package of credits for Bulgaria, but economists warn the Balkan country's severe economic problems will not be solved overnight.
Bulgaria's interim cabinet has agreed to tough conditions, including implementation of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime, to restore confidence in its collapsing currency.
But it must also tackle big foreign and domestic debt bills and a crumbling and illiquid banking system.

Ivan Kostov, leader of the Union of Democratic Forces which is expected to form the next government after elections next Saturday, said on Friday new agreements with the IMF and other donors would improve Bulgaria's financial discipline.

"Strict compliance will deal a blow against corruption, racketeering and unfair competition," he said, speaking as the IMF board met to approve the credit. "It will stop the chasing away of honest foreign and Bulgarian investors."
He said the accord would stimulate investment, "which means cash privatisation and new jobs", as well as lower emigration.
Bulgaria has also won pledges of $285 million from the European Commission, $115 million from the Group of 24 industrialised countries, and support from the World Bank.
Interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski said the total package would come to about $1.2 billion, which is little more than the $1 billion of foreign debt payments due this year.
Bulgaria is also seeking a rescheduling from the Paris Club of government creditors.

All political parties have declared their support for the reform programme, though the Bulgarian Socialist Party, which polls predict will form the main opposition in the new parliament, has criticised what it says is a lack of transparency over the negotiations.
The standby credit will provide $509 million over the next 14 months, while the remaining $148 million is an emergency credit for grain purchases.
Targets agreed by the interim cabinet and the IMF include reducing the budget deficit to 3.8 percent of GDP this year from last year's 12 percent.
Inflation, which was a cumulative 452.3 percent in the first three months, is expected to slow to reach 769 percent for the whole of 1997.

The National Statistics Institute expects unemployment, which was 13.7 percent of the workforce in February, to reach 17.7 percent by the end of the year as loss-making state enterprises are closed or restructured.
In June, the new government is expected to introduce a currency board, under which levs in circulation must be strictly matched to foreign currency reserves, putting strict limits on monetary policy.

The Economy Institute at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences warned on Monday that implementation would be difficult and painful and corrupt business interests could conspire to prevent the currency board from working.
